title: The Imaginary Axis and Frequency Response
intro: Set s = jω and the Laplace transform becomes the Fourier transform. Cutting the surface along the imaginary axis gives the frequency response, and reading it with a ruler shows why a pole near the axis makes a resonance and a zero on it makes a notch.

blocks.text: Slicing the surface
Put $\sigma = 0$ in the transform. The arrow $e^{-st}$ becomes $e^{-j\omega t}$, which neither grows nor shrinks, and

This is the Fourier transform of $x(t)$. It exists as an ordinary number whenever the imaginary axis is inside the region of convergence. The height of the surface along that line, $|X(j\omega)|$, says how much of the frequency $\omega$ rad/s the signal contains. If $x(t)$ is the impulse response of a system, it is the system's frequency response: the gain applied to a sinusoid of frequency $\omega$ passing through. The topic The Fourier Transform (#/math/fourier-transform) develops the Fourier side; here the axis is simply one line on a bigger map.

The viewer's lower-right panel draws this slice for $0 \le \omega \le 3$ rad/s, in decibels or in plain magnitude. Negative frequencies are left out: for a real signal, $X(-j\omega)$ is the complex conjugate of $X(j\omega)$, with the same size.
A pole, read from the axis
Take $x(t) = e^{-0.5t}u(t)$, so $X(s) = 1/(s + 0.5)$ and the axis is inside the region $\operatorname{Re} s > -0.5$. On the axis
That is one over the distance from the pole at $-0.5$ to the point $j\omega$. The values are in the table below, found by computing the square root and then $20\log_{10}$.

items: $\omega = 0$: $|X| = 2$, which is $6.02$ dB. The nearest point of the axis to the pole.

$\omega = 0.5$: $|X| = 1.414$, which is $3.01$ dB. The distance is $\sqrt{0.5} = 0.707$; the response has dropped to $1/\sqrt 2$ of its peak, the half-power point or $-3$ dB corner. It is at $\omega = a$, the pole's distance from the axis.

blocks.text: Well above the corner, the distance is nearly $\omega$ itself and the response is nearly $1/\omega$: doubling the frequency halves the height, which is $-6.02$ dB. From $\omega = 1.25$ to $2.5$ the actual drop is $5.55$ dB, approaching $6.02$ as $\omega$ grows. Engineers draw this on logarithmic axes and call it a Bode plot: a flat line to the corner, then a slope of $-20$ dB per factor of ten in frequency. The viewer's frequency axis is linear and only reaches 3, so you see the corner and the start of the slope but not the straight-line asymptote.
The phase is read from the angle of the arrow from the pole to the point: $-45^\circ$ at the corner $\omega = 0.5$ and $-80.5^\circ$ at $\omega = 3$. The viewer draws only the magnitude.

widget.title: A single pole and its response

blocks.text: With Probe frequency ω at 0.5 the response panel marks $3.01$ dB, 3 dB under the $6.02$ dB it has at $\omega = 0$. Drag ω to 0 and to 3 and compare with the table: $6.02$ dB and $-9.66$ dB. Then drag Decay rate a: a larger $a$ moves the pole further from the axis; the whole slice gets lower and flatter (at $a = 2$ the value at $\omega = 0$ is $1/2 = -6$ dB). A smaller $a$ brings the pole near the axis and the slice at low frequencies rises. Press Sweep ω and watch the violet pole line from the pole to the red probe grow and shrink.
A pole pair near the axis: resonance

A conjugate pair of poles at $-a \pm j\omega_0$ gives the damped sine $e^{-at}\sin(\omega_0 t)u(t)$. When $a$ is small the pole at $-a + j\omega_0$ is close to the axis point $j\omega_0$, so $1/d$ is large there and the response has a peak. Its height is about $1/(2a)$, since the near distance is $a$ and the far one is about $2\omega_0$, which the gain $\omega_0$ cancels. In numbers, for $\omega_0 = 1.5$:

items: $a = 0.5$: the peak is at $\omega = 1.414$ and has height $1.00$ (0 dB).
$a = 0.2$: the peak is at $\omega = 1.487$ and has height $2.50$ ($7.96$ dB).
$a = 0.1$: the peak is at $\omega = 1.497$ and has height $5.00$ ($13.98$ dB).

blocks.text: Halving $a$ doubles the height and narrows the peak. Setting the slope of $|X|^2$ to zero puts the peak at $\omega = \sqrt{\omega_0^2 - a^2}$, a little below $\omega_0$ ($\sqrt{2.25 - 0.25} = 1.414$ for $a = 0.5$), and it closes in on $\omega_0 = 1.5$ as $a$ falls. Making the poles approach the axis is what makes a tuned circuit ring for a long time and respond strongly to one frequency: that is a resonance. In the time signal the same $a$ sets how slowly the oscillation dies; see Pole Positions and the Time Signal (#/math/laplace-transform/poles-and-time).

In magnitude mode the slice rises to a clear peak at about $\omega = 1.5$ with height $2.5$ (the response panel runs from 0 to 5). Set Decay rate a to 0.1 and it reaches the top of the panel, $5.0$; set it to 0.5 and it flattens to $1.0$. Sweep ω from 0 and watch the red marker ride up the peak and down again. Tilt to 85° and compare the pole spots with the axis: the closer they are to the line $\sigma = 0$, the taller the peak.
A zero on the axis: a notch

A zero that lies on the imaginary axis forces $X(j\omega) = 0$ at that frequency: nothing at that frequency gets through. The notch filter of the viewer, $X(s) = (s^2 + \omega_0^2)/(s^2 + 0.75s + \omega_0^2)$ with $\omega_0 = 1.5$, has zeros at $\pm j1.5$ and poles at $-0.375 \pm j1.452$, just beside them. The zeros kill $1.5$ rad/s exactly; the poles beside them, of about the same distance from the axis point, make the dip narrow, because away from the notch they almost cancel.

With the ruler: at $\omega = 1.4$ the distances to the two zeros are $0.1$ and $2.9$, and to the two poles $0.379$ and $2.877$, so $|X| = (0.1 \times 2.9)/(0.379 \times 2.877) = 0.266$, which is $-11.5$ dB. At $\omega = 1.5$ the first zero distance is $0$ and so is the height. Far from the notch the height returns to 1: $|X(j0)| = 1$ (0 dB), $|X(j1)| = 0.858$ ($-1.34$ dB), $|X(j2)| = 0.759$ ($-2.39$ dB), $|X(j3)| = 0.949$ ($-0.46$ dB).

Probe frequency ω is at 1.4, where the response is $-11.5$ dB; the walk-through's ruler step should show the zero distances $0.10$ and $2.90$. Drag ω slowly through 1.5: the response panel plunges to the $-30$ dB floor there and comes back out, at $\omega = 1.6$ to $-12.0$ dB. In the 3D view the zeros are the pits sitting on the axis line, with the pole peaks right beside them. Change Frequency ω₀ to move the notch.
When the axis is the edge of the ROC

The unit step $u(t)$ has $X(s) = 1/s$, with the region $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$. The pole is at the origin and the axis is exactly the edge of the region. Along it $|X(j\omega)| = 1/\omega$: $2$ at $\omega = 0.5$, $1$ at 1, $0.5$ at 2, $0.333$ at 3 (that is $6.02$, $0$, $-6.02$ and $-9.54$ dB), falling 6 dB per doubling all the way. It is a valid slice but not the full Fourier transform: at $\omega = 0$ the pole makes it infinite, and the true Fourier transform of $u(t)$ also has an impulse $\pi\delta(\omega)$ there. The viewer words this as the Fourier transform existing only in a limiting sense. Push the pole to the right of the axis (a growing exponential, $a < 0$) and the axis is outside the region: the slice is still plotted from the formula, but the integral does not converge on it and the viewer says the Fourier transform does not exist.

This is the difference between the Laplace transform and the Fourier transform: the Laplace transform has the room to describe growing signals, and the Fourier transform is what it looks like on the one line that needs the signal to settle. For the same idea in discrete time, with the circle $|z| = 1$ in place of the axis, see The Unit Circle and Frequency Response (#/math/z-transform/unit-circle).
Problems

blocks.title: Corner frequency
blocks.text: A system has $H(s) = 4/(s + 4)$. What is $|H(j\omega)|$ at $\omega = 0$, at $\omega = 4$, and at $\omega = 16$? Where is the $-3$ dB corner?
solution: $|H(j\omega)| = 4/\sqrt{16 + \omega^2}$. At $\omega = 0$ it is $1$. At $\omega = 4$ it is $4/\sqrt{32} = 0.707$, which is $-3.01$ dB. At $\omega = 16$ it is $4/\sqrt{272} = 0.243$, which is $-12.3$ dB.
The corner is where the distance from the pole to the point is $\sqrt2$ times its minimum, which is at $\omega = 4$, the pole's distance from the axis.

blocks.title: Resonant peak
blocks.text: A damped sine has poles at $-0.05 \pm j2$. Estimate the height of the peak of the response of $2/\bigl((s+0.05)^2 + 4\bigr)$ at $\omega = 2$.
solution: The gain is $K = 2$. At $s = j2$ the near pole is at distance $0.05$ and the far pole $-0.05 - j2$ is at distance $|0.05 + j4| = 4.0003$. So $|X| = 2/(0.05 \times 4.0003) = 10.0$, which is $20$ dB. It agrees with $1/(2a) = 10$.

blocks.title: Where is the dip?
blocks.text: A filter has zeros at $\pm j5$. At which frequency is $|H(j\omega)|$ exactly zero, and does a zero at $-2$ create a dip on the axis?
solution: The zeros at $\pm j5$ lie on the axis, so $H(j5) = 0$: complete blocking at $5$ rad/s. A zero at $-2$ is off the axis; the distance from it to the axis never falls below $2$, so $|H|$ gets smaller near $\omega = 0$ but never reaches zero.
blocks.answer: Exactly zero at $\omega = 5$ rad/s; a zero at $-2$ gives only a mild dip.
